newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Castrol going strong in China.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Castrol going strong in China.

text.p: Burmah Castrol Plc said it is making strong progress in China's lubricants market, where it is a relative newcomer fighting giants like Exxon and Mobil.
The British company said it is firmly establishing itself in the upper segment of the market by selling top brand, high margin products.
"Relative to our competitors, we are getting better quality growth," Castrol director Ian Pringle told Reuters on Tuesday. "We believe our progress is really, really good," he added.
Pringle is in charge of the rapidly expanding Asia-Pacific lubricants business, which contributed 27 percent of group operating profit last year.
Burmah already has a notably strong position in South East Asia, while it is seeking to raise market shares in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.
Asia as a whole is Burmah Castrol's success story as the group continues to beat the region's overall growth.
While the Asian lubricants market is increasing by six to seven percent per year, Castrol saw its volumes rise by about 10 percent last year.
This growth rate will likely be maintained in 1997, Pringle said. "We expect that sort of rate to continue," he said.
Pringle is based in Hong Kong, but came over for a short visit to Burmah Castrol's headquarters.

His message is that it is business as usual in Hong Kong after the territory's handover to China four weeks ago. Pringle, who helped set up the Hong Kong office early last year, said Burmah Castrol never feared the change of power.
"I cannot see how you can be serious about China and worry about living in Hong Kong," he said.
Burmah Castrol is already active in Shanghai and the Guangdong province, where it is constructing a joint venture lubricant plant.
The company started only five years ago with seriously building up its position in China. Competitors such as Exxon Corp, Shell and Mobil Corp were already active there for a long time.
But Castrol is making up ground quickly as strong economic growth in southern China in particular means greater demand for Castrol's relatively expensive brand products.
"As the market is growing, the sophistication is increasing and that is playing into our strength." Pringle said.
He added Castrol's business is also roaring ahead in other parts of Asia Pacific except for mature markets such as New Zealand and Australia.
But in another mature market -- Japan -- Castrol is moving ahead amid good demand for its premium products, Pringle said.
Asia was the main motor behind Burmah Castrol's 10 percent earnings growth in 1996 when profits after tax totalled 148.7 million stg.
But analysts see flat to slightly lower results this year because of the sterling's persistent strength.
This, however, fails to upset Pringle, who pointed to the strong underlying performance in local currency terms.
"We are very bullish about growth prospects in all of our (Asian) territories," Pringle said.
